strengths: Introduces a large-scale (1M+) and diverse MER training dataset (UniMER-1M) spanning simple printed, complex printed, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions, substantially larger and more varied than prior datasets like IM2LATEX-100K and Pix2tex.

Proposes UniMER-Test, a well-structured benchmark with four distinct evaluation dimensions (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE) that better reflects real-world MER challenges than existing benchmarks focused mainly on simple printed or handwritten expressions.
The Length-Aware Module is a reasonable and lightweight architectural addition, with an ablation (Table 4) showing consistent gains especially on complex/long expressions (CPE).

Extensive experiments including ablations on data composition, augmentation, and LAM, plus comparisons against both printed-formula SOTA (Pix2tex, Texify) and handwritten-formula SOTA (CAN, SAN, CoMER, etc.) on standard CROHME/HME100K benchmarks, showing consistent improvements.
Data augmentation strategy (weather noise, dilation/erosion, etc.) is shown empirically to meaningfully help on noisy/screen-captured data (SCE), addressing a practically important robustness gap.
The dataset and benchmark, if released as claimed, could be a genuinely useful community resource given the scarcity of diverse, large-scale MER data.
weaknesses: Technical description of the Length-Aware Module is vague: it is unclear how length is discretized/represented (is it a classification over C length bins, or a regression?), how ground-truth length labels are obtained/binned, and how the length embedding is combined with token/position embeddings (concatenation vs. addition) — insufficient detail for reproducibility.

The performance gain from LAM alone is quite small and only clearly beneficial on CPE (+2% BLEU), with negligible or slightly negative effects on other subsets (Table 4), raising questions about how much the module truly contributes versus data/augmentation, which appear to be the dominant factors.

Dataset construction methodology lacks critical detail: for SCE, only 4,744 test formulas were manually collected/verified via Mathpix + human correction (no SCE training data appears to be described distinctly, raising concerns about train/test distribution match for this subset); details about de-duplication and any train/test leakage checks (e.g., overlap between web/Arxiv sourced formulas in UniMER-1M and existing test sets) are not provided.

No statistical significance testing or repeated runs are reported; single-run results are used for all comparisons and ablations, which is a common but limiting practice given some improvements are marginal (e.g., LAM contribution).

Comparisons with LVLM-based approaches (Nougat, Vary) are only qualitative (Fig. 5, three samples) rather than quantitative on the full UniMER-Test benchmark, weakening the claim that they are only outperformed by UniMERNet.

The writing has some clarity issues and minor grammatical errors, and cross-references between sections/tables occasionally lack precision (e.g., exact number of SCE training samples used is not explicitly stated).

Novelty of the core architectural contribution (LAM: self-attention + global pooling + length regression fed as embedding) is incremental relative to existing counting/length-aware modules such as CAN's counting module, and the paper's justification for why it is more suitable for LaTeX (vs. CAN's symbol counting) is somewhat hand-wavy rather than empirically isolated.
The dataset and code availability is only promised ('available at') with no working link provided in the reviewed manuscript, limiting reproducibility assessment at this stage.

strengths: The UniMER-1M training set (1,061,791 samples) and UniMER-Test benchmark (23,789 samples spanning SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE) represent a genuinely larger and more diverse resource than prior MER datasets (Im2Latex-100K, Pix2tex, CROHME, HME100K), and the explicit inclusion of screen-captured and long/complex printed expressions addresses a real gap in existing benchmarks.

The paper provides reasonably thorough ablations (training data composition, augmentation, LAM) and head-to-head comparisons against several open-source baselines (Pix2tex, Texify, Nougat) and HMER-specific SOTA models (CAN, SAN, CoMER, BTTR) across multiple test sets.

The reported overall results show clear improvements over compared open baselines across the four proposed test subsets, and the data construction pipeline (regularization, multi-DPI rendering, length-balanced sampling) is described in enough detail to be partially reproducible.
weaknesses: The core architectural novelty (Length-Aware Module) provides only marginal and inconsistent benefit: in Table 4, adding LAM improves CPE BLEU by ~2% but slightly *worsens* SPE (BLEU 0.918→0.917, EditDis 0.056→0.058) and gives negligible change on SCE/HWE, which is weak evidence for a module positioned as a central contribution.

The backbone (Swin encoder + mBART decoder) is directly adopted from Donut, so the architectural contribution beyond the auxiliary length-regression head is limited; most of the performance gain over baselines appears attributable to the much larger/more diverse UniMER-1M training data rather than to the proposed network design, but the paper does not disentangle this cleanly (e.g., no experiment training a baseline architecture on UniMER-1M vs. UniMERNet on UniMER-1M to isolate the architecture's own contribution).

There are internal inconsistencies in the reported numbers that raise reproducibility/correctness concerns: e.g., in Table 3 the Pix2tex (no augmentation) row reports HWE BLEU=0.087 but EditDis=0.004, which is implausible given such a low BLEU score and is inconsistent with the EditDis=0.775 reported for the same configuration in Table 2; this is either a typo or an unexplained discrepancy that undermines confidence in the empirical results.

The qualitative comparison with LVLMs (Nougat, Vary) in Section 5.4 is limited to three cherry-picked examples with no quantitative benchmark numbers, which is insufficient evidence to support claims that LVLMs perform only 'mediocre' MER relative to UniMERNet.

Dataset construction for the SCE subset relies on a commercial third-party OCR engine (Mathpix) for initial annotation followed by manual correction, which raises questions about annotation quality control (e.g., inter-annotator agreement is not reported) and about licensing/redistribution of such data.

No statistical significance testing, variance across runs, or confidence intervals are reported for any of the benchmark comparisons, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (e.g., 1-5 point ExpRate improvements) are robust versus incidental.

Table and figure presentation has avoidable errors/ambiguities (e.g., Table 2's caption states it shows 'models using different augmentations' but the table content is actually a training-data ablation, duplicating the content of the text; Fig. 1's bar labeling is confusingly laid out), which reduce clarity.

The related-work section is largely an enumerative list of prior methods without critical synthesis connecting them to the specific design choices of UniMERNet, limiting the paper's positioning relative to closely related transformer-based MER/document models.

The dataset/model availability link in the abstract is left blank in the manuscript, and reproducibility details (e.g., exact augmentation parameters, full hyperparameters for baselines retrained on UniMER-1M) are only partially specified.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale, diverse MER training dataset (UniMER-1M, ~1M samples) that substantially exceeds prior open datasets in scale and formula-length diversity, addressing a real gap in existing benchmarks that focus mainly on simple printed or handwritten expressions.

Proposes UniMER-Test, a well-structured four-way benchmark (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE) that enables fine-grained, real-world-relevant evaluation of MER robustness across formula complexity, noise, and handwriting styles -- a genuinely useful community resource.

The Length-Aware Module is a simple, well-motivated architectural addition, and its benefit is empirically isolated via ablation (Table 4), showing consistent gains particularly on complex/long formulas (CPE).

Extensive experiments span comparisons against printed-formula specialists (Pix2tex, Texify), handwritten-formula SOTA methods (CAN, SAN, CoMER, etc.), and qualitative failure-case analysis against LVLM-based approaches (Nougat), providing a fairly comprehensive validation across scenario types.

Ablations cleanly decompose the contribution of data scale/diversity, image augmentation, and LAM, allowing readers to attribute performance gains to each component rather than treating the system as a monolithic black box.
Dataset and model release (data/code availability stated) supports reproducibility and community adoption.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core architecture is a standard Swin+mBART encoder-decoder (borrowed from Donut), and the Length-Aware Module is a relatively simple auxiliary length-regression head with modest reported gains (e.g., +2% BLEU on CPE, negligible/mixed on other subsets in Table 4); the primary contribution is arguably the dataset rather than the modeling innovation.

Data collection methodology has limited transparency: the regularization/augmentation pipeline for expanding SPE/CPE via Arxiv/Wikipedia/StackExchange is described only briefly, with no analysis of potential duplicate/near-duplicate leakage between train and test splits, LaTeX rendering diversity (fonts/styles), or quality control beyond 'uncompilable expressions discarded.'

SCE test set construction relies on Mathpix-generated pseudo-labels with only two annotators for manual correction and cross-verification; annotation agreement/quality metrics are not reported, raising concerns about label reliability for this crucial 'real-world noisy' subset where performance gaps are largest.

No statistical significance testing or variance across runs is reported for any of the comparison tables, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements (especially smaller ones, e.g., LAM ablation) are robust versus noise.

The comparison with LVLM-based methods (Nougat, Vary) is only qualitative (three cherry-picked examples in Fig. 5) rather than quantitative on the full UniMER-Test benchmark, weakening the claim that these methods are decisively inferior.

The paper does not discuss computational cost/inference speed trade-offs of adding the LAM and heavier data augmentation, nor model size comparisons with baselines, limiting assessment of practical deployment trade-offs.

Limited discussion of failure modes or error analysis for UniMERNet itself; the paper mostly showcases wins in Fig. 5 without deeper analysis of remaining error categories (e.g., very long formulas, specific symbol confusions).

strengths: Introduces a large-scale (1M+ sample) MER training dataset (UniMER-1M) that is substantially larger and more diverse than prior datasets like IM2LATEX-100K and Pix2tex, spanning simple, complex, screen-captured, and handwritten formulas.
Proposes UniMER-Test, a well-constructed and diverse benchmark (SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE) that better reflects real-world MER challenges than existing narrow benchmarks, addressing a genuine gap in the field.

The architectural modifications (Fine-Grained Embedding, ConvEnhance, Removal of Shift Window, Squeeze Attention) are simple, well-motivated, and empirically validated via systematic ablations (Tables 2, 3, 6-9), showing consistent accuracy and speed improvements over a Texify/Swin/mBART baseline.

Extensive experiments, including comparisons with SOTA (Pix2tex, Texify, Nougat), pretraining ablations, and depth/architecture sensitivity studies, provide reasonably thorough empirical support for the claims.

The dataset construction pipeline (deduplication via perceptual hashing, LaTeX normalization, balanced length sampling, diverse rendering fonts/DPIs, data augmentation strategy) is described in good technical detail, aiding reproducibility.
Practical utility: the resulting model and dataset appear directly useful for real-world document/formula extraction pipelines, and the paper reports plans for public release of data/models/code.
weaknesses: Novelty of the architectural contributions is incremental: FGE, ConvEnhance, and Squeeze Attention are relatively straightforward adaptations of existing ideas (overlapping conv patch embedding, depthwise conv enhancement, low-rank/bottleneck attention) already explored in the vision transformer literature; the core contribution is largely the dataset rather than fundamentally new modeling insight.

SCE test set is quite small (4,744 samples) and was annotated/corrected by only two annotators with Mathpix-assisted labeling, raising potential concerns about annotation quality, bias, and statistical robustness of results on this most 'real-world' subset.

The comparison with Nougat is potentially unfair/awkward — the paper notes it had to synthetically embed formulas in random text to accommodate Nougat's page-level design, which may not reflect Nougat's true intended use case, weakening the validity of that qualitative comparison.

Reported BLEU improvements on some subsets (e.g., SPE) are marginal (0.9%), and the paper does not report statistical significance or variance across multiple runs, making it hard to assess whether gains are robust or within noise.

Limited discussion of failure cases or error analysis beyond three cherry-picked qualitative examples (Figure 5); no quantitative breakdown of error types (e.g., symbol confusion vs. structural errors) that would substantiate claims about the encoder's fine-grained/local advantages.

The 16M image-text pretraining corpus and additional 4M LaTeX source expansion data are not released or fully specified in terms of licensing/filtering, raising some reproducibility concerns for the pretraining stage results (Table 6).

The paper's claim of 'first study on MER targeting complex real-world scenarios' is a strong claim that somewhat overlooks related large-scale document understanding efforts (e.g., Nougat, Vary) which also address real-world document/formula extraction, even if not MER-specialized; the framing could be more measured.
Some presentation issues: inconsistent test set sizes between Table 1 (23,757) and text (23,789), and dataset/table formatting typos, slightly undermining polish and clarity.

strengths: The UniMER-1M training set (1M+ LaTeX-image pairs) and UniMER-Test benchmark, spanning SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE categories, address a genuine gap in existing MER datasets (IM2LATEX, Pix2tex, CROHME), which are limited in scale, length distribution, and real-world noise/distortion coverage.

The ablation in Table 2 convincingly shows that training data diversity/scale (UniMER-1M vs Pix2tex/HWE) is the dominant factor in generalization across scenario types, which is a useful empirical finding for the community.

The architectural components (FGE, CE, RSW, SA) are reasonably motivated by task-specific characteristics (visual symbol similarity, spatial layout, decoding speed) and are evaluated via a systematic ablation (Table 3) including depth/throughput trade-off studies in the appendix.

Data construction details (deduplication via perceptual hashing for SCE, LaTeX normalization, rendering pipeline, data augmentation strategy) are documented thoroughly enough to support reproducibility of the dataset pipeline.
The reported speed-accuracy trade-off (UniMERNet-T is faster and still competitive) is practically useful for real-world deployment.
weaknesses: Despite extensive discussion of large vision-language models (Nougat, Vary) as competitors in the introduction and related work, no quantitative comparison with these models is provided in the main results (Table 5); only a small qualitative figure (Fig. 5) touches on Nougat, which is insufficient to substantiate claims that UniMERNet 'outperforms' the broader landscape of modern MER/LVLM approaches.

The architectural novelty is incremental: FGE (overlapping conv patch embedding), CE (depthwise conv blocks akin to CMT/ConViT), and SA (low-rank/bottleneck attention) are adaptations of existing techniques from the vision literature rather than fundamentally new ideas, and the ablation gains from these modules are often marginal (e.g., Table 3 HWE BLEU is essentially flat or slightly decreases with SA/full configuration vs. partial configurations).

The paper claims 'first study' targeting real-world MER scenarios, but this is an overreach given that Nougat and Vary already target real-world document/formula extraction, and prior HMER works already address noisy handwritten inputs; the novelty claim should be tempered.

ExpRate is introduced as an evaluation metric but is never reported in any table, leaving an announced evaluation axis unused and the evaluation protocol feels incomplete relative to its own stated metrics.

The SCE test-set ground truth relies on Mathpix (a commercial black-box OCR tool) plus manual correction by only two annotators; no inter-annotator agreement or error-rate analysis is reported, raising concerns about label quality and potential systematic bias inherited from Mathpix.

The large accuracy gaps in Table 5 (e.g., Texify's very low SCE/HWE scores vs. Texify* retrained on UniMER-1M) show the comparisons against 'baseline' competitor models are confounded by training data differences rather than isolating architectural contribution, making the headline 'UniMERNet outperforms SOTA' claim partly attributable to the dataset rather than the proposed network.

Presentation issues remain (e.g., 'designe' and 'piratical' typos in the conclusion, awkward self-citation of the dataset as (He et al. 2024) in a seemingly non-anonymized reference), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread.
No statistical variance/multiple-run reporting is provided for any metric, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements (sometimes <1 BLEU point) are meaningful or within noise.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale (1M+) and notably diverse MER training corpus (UniMER-1M) spanning simple/complex printed, screen-captured, and handwritten formulas, addressing a genuine gap in prior benchmarks that were largely limited to simple printed or handwritten expressions.

UniMER-Test is thoughtfully constructed with four distinct sub-categories (SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE) that better reflect real-world deployment conditions (noisy scans, screenshots, long/multi-line formulas), providing a more discriminative and practically relevant benchmark than existing test sets.

Extensive and systematic ablations are provided: dataset composition (Table 2), each architectural component (Table 3), pretraining with text-image pairs (Table 6), data augmentation (Table 7), and encoder/decoder depth trade-offs (Tables 8-9), giving good insight into what drives the reported gains.

Clear practical value: the proposed encoder/decoder modifications (FGE, ConvEnhance, RSW, Squeeze Attention) yield simultaneous accuracy and throughput improvements over a strong baseline (Texify) trained on the same data, and multiple model sizes (T/S/B) are offered for different speed/accuracy trade-offs.

Reasonable engineering detail on dataset curation (LaTeX normalization, rendering fonts/DPI variety, perceptual-hash deduplication for SCE, augmentation pipeline), which aids reproducibility, with code/data/models promised to be released.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: overlapping-kernel patch embedding, depthwise convolution enhancement interleaved with attention, and removing shift-window are all established ideas from prior conv-transformer hybrid work (CMT, ConViT, CPE) applied to a new task rather than fundamentally new mechanisms; Squeeze Attention is a straightforward low-rank/bottleneck projection on Q/K.

Individual component ablations in Table 3 show quite small isolated gains (e.g., FGE alone changes BLEU by ~0.000-0.005), so the claimed benefit of some modules rests mainly on their combination, which weakens the case for each module's individual contribution.

The SCE test set (4,744 samples) is comparatively small and was labeled via Mathpix OCR plus manual correction by only two annotators; no inter-annotator agreement or independent verification against ground-truth LaTeX source is reported, raising some concern about label reliability for this key real-world subset.

Comparisons with LVLM baselines (Nougat, Vary) are somewhat uneven — Nougat is designed for full-page understanding and the paper manually appends random text to adapt test images, which is a reasonable workaround but introduces an ad hoc evaluation protocol that is not fully controlled or discussed quantitatively (only shown qualitatively in Fig. 5).

BLEU and Edit Distance, while standard, have known limitations for LaTeX (syntactic variability), and ExpRate — introduced in the metrics section — is not actually reported in the main comparison tables, leaving an announced evaluation axis unused.

The claim of being the "first study" targeting real-world MER is a strong framing given related efforts (Nougat, Vary, Texify) already attempt real-world document/formula extraction; the distinction is more about a more comprehensive benchmark and dataset scale than being the first work in this space.

No statistical variance (multiple runs/seeds) is reported for the main results, so the magnitude of some reported improvements (e.g., single-digit BLEU point gains from individual ablation components) cannot be assessed for robustness.
